output:
*Interview with Félix Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Monsieur Monnier, thank you for waiting. Tell me about the dinner, as much as you remember.

FÉLIX: Remember it? My uncle would not let anyone forget it. When the temple bell struck nine, my watch showed twenty minutes to nine, and he made a scene about it in front of everyone. He said it was a disgrace, and he was not wrong, but he never asked to look at it properly. It is my father's silver watch. He died in 1889, and I have never let anyone regulate it, not even Uncle Aurèle. It has always been troublesome. Aunt Odile was embarrassed for me, Dr Vauthier made a joke, and Girard laughed into his glass.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

FÉLIX: I went up to the library and stayed there alone. I had brandy, several glasses, I will be honest. I was upset, and I did not want to sit in the salon and be looked at. I owe money to a great many people, Inspector, some of it to Bastien Girard, which I suppose you know already.

MATTHEY: Go on, when you are ready.

FÉLIX: At a quarter past ten by my watch, someone went quickly up the stairs past the library door. I did not see who. The door was shut. Then at twenty-one minutes past ten by my watch, someone came quickly down. Again I did not see who. I thought nothing of it then.

MATTHEY: Did you hear anything else?

FÉLIX: At eighteen minutes past ten by my watch I heard a thump on the floor right above me, in the atelier. Right above me, Inspector. The library ceiling is his pine floor. And then my uncle's repeater sounding. I know that sound as well as I know my own name. He used to make us listen to it. Ten slow deep notes, I counted those, then some doubled notes, then quick high ones that I did not count. I stopped counting. I sat there with my hand over my mouth.

MATTHEY: What did you think the thump was?

FÉLIX: I thought he had dropped a tool. What else would I think? I was downstairs with a bottle.

MATTHEY: Who came to the library next?

FÉLIX: Bastien Girard came in at thirty-two minutes past ten by my watch. He came in without knocking, the way he does, and sat down. We sat together there until the temple struck eleven. He wanted to buy the rights to the repeater. They had quarrelled about the price at dinner, and he wanted to talk about it again. I told him my uncle would never sell. We drank.

MATTHEY: Did Monsieur Girard speak of anything else?

FÉLIX: Only money, which with Bastien is everything. He does not like Dr Vauthier, and he does not like me much either, but he sat with me, and I was grateful.

FÉLIX: I know how this looks. I was alone below the atelier with a thump over my head and then the repeater. Everyone will say that. And I am the heir. My uncle has looked after me since my father died, out of duty, I think, not affection. He would have cut me off if he could have. I did not hurt him. I was downstairs.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Monsieur Monnier. Please remain in the house.

FÉLIX: Of course. Inspector, will you tell Aunt Odile I was not drunk when the bell struck? I was only frightened.
